questions.title: Criminal liability and the resolution of conflicting evidence

scores.name: Grounding & citation discipline
scores.justification: The answer usually anchors propositions to document numbers and parts, and is appropriately cautious about disputed provenance, device attribution and privilege. However, it makes a serious grounding failure by stating that D01 was supplied only through paragraph 21 and that it therefore could not see paragraph 25: the full bundle contains D01 paragraphs 21–34, including paragraph 25. It also does not consistently pin each factual proposition to a precise paragraph, and occasionally turns contested material into a stronger proposition than the source permits.
evidence: D01 para.25 expressly records the £4,500 payments and says HSE was informed on 2 May 2024
Answer: “The supplied extract of D01 available for this advice contains paragraphs 1-21 but not paragraph 25”
D09 Part 2: examiner cannot exclude re-typing of a genuine earlier certificate
D11 para.4.1: account/device attribution does not establish physical composition of a message

scores.name: Contradiction identification
scores.justification: The answer usefully identifies the core D04/D05 conflict, the weak provenance of Version A, the suspension/resumption timing conflict, the site-wind/Met Office disparity, the expert disagreement and the NVR-ticket inconsistency. Its treatment of the crane logger as more probative than recollection or an altered manuscript log is particularly sound. But it does not identify and rank at least fifteen distinct contradictions, and it does not state which evidence is more probative and why for each conflict; it also misses several expressly planted contradictions, including D01 paragraph 25 versus D05 paragraphs 13–14, the D10/D20.3 inconsistency about seeking return of item 10.6, and the erroneous ‘eleven days’ statement in D13 when set against the D18 dates.
evidence: D14 Parts 1–2: struck-through 11:05 resumption entry versus machine-recorded resumption at 11:13:26
D01 para.25: neither Pyle statement discloses payments; D05 paras.13–14 expressly does disclose them
D10 disclosure note: solicitors demanded return of item 10.6; D20.3 final bullet says Meridian has not sought its return
D13 Part 4: installation said to be eleven days after disclosure; D18.1 dates the email 16 November and HSE call 17 November, while equipment was installed 1 December
D06 paras.13 and 24: the wording and amendment concerning resumption required separate treatment

scores.name: Legal accuracy & authority
scores.justification: The statutory corporate-manslaughter route, the distinction between corporate and personal gross-negligence liability, and the s.37 consent/connivance/neglect route are broadly accurate. Bilta, Singularis and Sellu are real authorities and are linked, and the answer correctly explains that the 2007 Act contains a specific senior-management test rather than relying on ordinary agency attribution. However, it does not address or cite Argent and Howell despite the question expressly requiring regard to the solicitor’s note that invokes them, and it does not explain the ‘so far as is reasonably practicable’ character of the proposed underlying HSWA s.3 offence.
evidence: D16.3 names Bilta (UK) Ltd v Nazir (No.2) and Singularis Holdings Ltd v Daiwa Capital Markets Europe Ltd
D07 solicitor’s note expressly invokes R v Argent and R v Howell
D01 para.28 identifies evidence capable of breaches of HSWA ss.2(1) and 3(1)
Answer correctly distinguishes s.1(3) senior-management liability from Ferris’s own-duty gross-negligence route

scores.name: Reasoning in the alternative
scores.justification: This is one of the stronger aspects of the answer. It repeatedly identifies alternative possibilities: whether Delacroix-Hale was statutory senior management, whether Version A followed remedial work after Version B, whether the photo/badge evidence proves Ferris’s presence, and whether Danecourt’s dynamic analysis redirects immediate causation. It also specifies sensible enquiries capable of resolving several forks. The deduction reflects the unsupported assertion that D01 paragraph 25 was unavailable, which prevented proper alternative analysis of the direct documentary conflict over disclosure of Pyle’s payments.
evidence: D08 Part 3: Version B defect record and Version A satisfactory handover are not logically inconsistent if remedial work occurred, though no repair record exists
D13 Parts 1–2: visitor badge and image metadata permit competing inferences about Ferris’s presence
D20.1 paras.4–6: dynamic analysis produces a materially different causal account
D01 para.34: it remains unestablished which drawing revision was on site on 14 November

scores.name: Asserted vs said vs shown vs established
scores.justification: The answer generally distinguishes witness accounts, party contentions, machine records, expert opinions and what can safely be inferred. It is notably careful in saying that the crane record proves resumption but not the decision-maker, and that the deleted-message evidence does not prove message content or personal authorship. Some language nevertheless overstates the position, notably the opening reference to ‘admitted’ absence of ties and the treatment of some alleged system failures as existing rather than as matters capable of proof.
evidence: D14 Part 2: crane record is machine-generated but contains no identity of the person authorising the lift
D11 paras.2.1–2.6 and 4.1: deleted-message pattern is unexplained and authorship is not proved
D20.1 para.1: Danecourt says the missing ties are established by the HSE survey
D01 paras.14–15: HSE makes no finding on which inspection record or certificate is authentic

scores.name: Determinative silences
scores.justification: The answer identifies a number of genuinely determinative missing matters, including radio material, governance/delegation evidence, the missing original records, and evidence capable of resolving device and location attribution. It also proposes proportionate enquiries for them. It does not, however, clearly organise these as at least three bundle silences and explain in each instance why the absence is determinative; it overlooks, for example, the unidentified agency operatives and missing Northgate assignment records.
evidence: D01 para.9: two agency operatives are unidentified and Northgate’s assignment records cannot be located
D01 para.19: HSE has not resolved who, if anyone, decided to continue lifting
D08 Part 3: no repair record, materials requisition or identified operative
D14 Part 2: the crane driver was not asked to undertake voice comparison

scores.name: Completeness
scores.justification: All five numbered parts of Q1 receive substantial treatment, including the requested forum distinction and the distinction between the corporate and individual routes. The advice nevertheless fails to answer the required D01 paragraph 25 aspect because it incorrectly treats that paragraph as unseen, and its contradiction analysis does not meet the expressly required fifteen-conflict exercise. The length of the further-enquiry list does not cure those omissions.
evidence: Question 1.2 specifically requires treatment of D01 para.25
D01 para.25 is present in the supplied full bundle
Answer’s ‘Further enquiries’ item 8 asks to obtain material already in the bundle

questions.overallComment: The advice is strongest on legal structure, conditional reasoning about causation, and the evidential limits of the crane and digital records. Its central defect is a demonstrably false assertion that D01 paragraph 25 was unavailable, causing it to miss a material contradiction concerning Pyle’s payments. It also falls well short of the required systematic identification and probative ranking of at least fifteen contradictions. The result is an analytically capable but insufficiently bundle-disciplined prosecution advice.

questions.title: The commercial and insurance consequences

scores.name: Grounding & citation discipline
scores.justification: The answer usually gives useful document references and correctly treats a number of matters as allegations or provisional evidence. However, it asserts an unsupported present date of 12 September 2026 and unsupported immediate knowledge by Mr Aksoy of all material defendants, then derives an urgent limitation conclusion from those assertions. More seriously, it says substantial bundle documents were "Not Yet Reviewed", including D15 Part 4, D08 and D11-D14, although those documents are in the supplied bundle and D15 Part 4 is extensively relied on elsewhere in the answer; that is a direct grounding failure under the stated instruction.
evidence: Answer: "Limitation as at 12 September 2026"; no bundle document supplies that date.
Answer: "Mr Aksoy knew immediately ... who the material potential defendants were"; D03 records his later civil claim but not immediate knowledge.
Answer, Not Yet Reviewed: "D15 Part 4"; D15 Part 4 contains VM/1 and is reproduced in full.
Answer, Not Yet Reviewed: D08, D11, D12, D13 and D14; each is reproduced in full in the bundle.

scores.name: Contradiction identification
scores.justification: The answer identifies the late Pay Less Notice, the certificate/metadata tension, and the funding-period arithmetic, but it does not identify fifteen distinct contradictions or state a reasoned probative ranking for each. Its certification discussion correctly recognises that VM/1 and the fraud material are not logically irreconcilable, but that is not a substitute for the required contradiction analysis. It entirely misses numerous planted conflicts, including the D10/D20.3 return-demand inconsistency, D06 paragraph 13's internal inconsistency, the struck-through 11:05 log against the machine-generated crane chronology, the two D08 records, and the D13/D18 timing problem.

scores.name: Legal accuracy & authority
scores.justification: The statutory treatment of fair presentation, proportionate remedies, sections 10-12, section 17, CDM duties, the Third Parties Act and Fatal Accidents Act is generally competent, and the answer accurately cites Versloot and Gosvenor. But it invents and relies on an unverified authority, "Oakland Wantage Care Home Ltd v Stepnell Ltd" [2026] EWHC/TCC/1530, including an asserted holding. It also fails the express requirement to provide resolved citations, or an express distinction, for the named Grove, Bexheat and SG South authorities; referring generically to a "line" is insufficient.

scores.name: Reasoning in the alternative
scores.justification: The answer is strongest where it sets out alternatives: fraud proved or not proved for payment, valid or invalid termination under clause 8.4.4, and competing accounts of insurance formation and causation. It also correctly identifies the need to know what material the Coldbrook decision-maker actually had on 19 December, rather than retrospectively relying on the May 2024 metadata report. The score is reduced because it sometimes presents later-generated evidence, such as HSE's authenticated-drawing material, as support for Coldbrook's belief at the earlier date without showing that Coldbrook then possessed it, and silently assumes a present date for limitation.
evidence: D16.1 contains Coldbrook's 8 December allegation that TWDC-BW-07 was created on or about 13 November.
D17 Part 4: Northmoor's metadata report was served on 6 May 2024.

scores.name: Asserted vs said vs shown vs established
scores.justification: The answer generally distinguishes well between what Coldbrook says, what Meridian says, what an expert or HSE report records, and what the court would have to decide. It appropriately qualifies the metadata evidence, the Vellacott Marr certificate, and the held-covered email. There are nevertheless slippages: it calls the HSE-calculated load and safety findings "facts" in places despite D01's explicit preliminary and non-evidential status, and it occasionally treats the contents of Coldbrook's default notice as evidence of its underlying evidential basis rather than evidence only that the allegation was made.
evidence: D01 paragraph 1: conclusions are provisional.

scores.name: Determinative silences
scores.justification: The answer identifies more than three genuinely determinative evidential gaps and usually states what would resolve them. These include the missing text and service contents relevant to clause 4.7.4, the documents Vellacott Marr actually reviewed, Coldbrook's 19 December decision material, authority for TowerLine's alleged held-covered arrangement, and dependency and estate evidence. Those are appropriately treated as matters requiring disclosure or further enquiry rather than assumed facts.

scores.name: Completeness
scores.justification: All four numbered questions receive some substantive treatment, including the requested forum-specific Third Parties Act route and the common-law termination alternative. However, the answer expressly ends with a substantial "Not Yet Reviewed" list covering central causation, attribution, access, weather, lifting and payment records, despite the assessment requiring a complete answer and expressly directing a deduction for such a list. That omission also weakens the conclusions on termination, insurer defences and the personal-injury claims.
evidence: Answer, Not Yet Reviewed: D08-D14, D15 Part 4 and further D17 material.

D11 concerns Ferris/Delacroix-Hale messages and attribution.

questions.overallComment: This is a well-structured and often legally sensible piece of advice, particularly on the contractual service defect, the alternatives under clause 8.4.4, and the Insurance Act framework. Its central assessment failure is evidential discipline: it does not undertake the required comprehensive contradiction analysis and expressly disclaims review of documents that are present and material. The invented Oakland authority and the missing proper treatment of Grove, Bexheat and SG South are serious legal-authority defects. The limitation advice is also unsafe because it invents the date at which the advice is given and assumes immediate knowledge not established by the bundle.

questions.title: Admissibility, privilege, disclosure and professional conduct

scores.name: Grounding & citation discipline
scores.justification: The answer is usually careful to cite bundle items and to distinguish documents from allegations, particularly on the recording, the SMS and the expert-report material. However, it twice says that D20.3's contents must be inspected or are not available for a final ruling, then hypothesises that it might contain third-party or facilitative communications; the complete attendance note is reproduced at D20 p.5. That is a serious grounding failure on a central issue, because the actual note records Ferris's further question about producing the certificate without disclosing when it was made, as well as the solicitor's refusal.
evidence: D20 item 20.3, p.5: the full attendance note is reproduced, including Ferris's question about the certificate going to HSE "and nobody says anything about when it was made".
D20 item 20.3, p.5: "I have not been instructed to do anything and I have done nothing."
D10 item 10.6, pp.3-4: the contemporaneous email records substantially the same consultation and advice.

scores.name: Contradiction identification
scores.justification: The answer notices some inconsistencies, including D13's "eleven days" statement against the 16 and 17 November disclosures, the board-minute chronology, weather evidence, and the three possible readings of the audio. It does not identify fifteen distinct contradictions and, crucially, rarely states which source is more probative and why. It misses or inadequately handles planted conflicts including D10's return demand against D20.3's statement that Meridian had not sought return of item 10.6, the 11:05 struck-through resumption entry against the machine-generated 11:13:26 crane restart, and the inconsistency in D06 paragraph 13.
evidence: D13 Part 4 says installation was "eleven days after Ms Raghunathan's disclosure"; D18 item 18.1 and D01 para.20 identify 16 and 17 November disclosures and D13 records installation on 1 December.
D14 Part 1 records "Lifting ops resumed" at 11:05; D14 Part 2 records no hook load until 11:13:26.
D10 disclosure note, p.1, says return of item 10.6 was demanded on 11 April 2024; D20 item 20.3, p.5, says Meridian "has not sought the return of item 10.6".
D06 para.13 expressly accepts that "Are we still lifting??" is not consistent with the witness's claimed earlier suspension instruction.

scores.name: Legal accuracy & authority
scores.justification: There is useful statutory analysis of legal-advice privilege, CPR 35.4, CJA 2003 hearsay, GDPR Article 6(1)(f), ERA sections 43B, 43J, 47B and 103A, and the answer correctly distinguishes weight from admissibility in several places. But its central iniquity analysis is too categorical: a solicitor's refusal to advise a proposed fraud does not by itself prevent the exception applying where the client uses the consultation in furtherance of an intended dishonest presentation; D20.3 contains evidence capable of supporting that alternative. The answer does not accurately substantiate the specifically required authorities Cox and Railton, Eustice and Ablyazov, instead relying on additional, unverified recent authorities, and it wrongly says PACE section 78 applies throughout the United Kingdom. It also evades rather than resolves the DPA 2018 sections 35-40 point, and does not state the applicable burden analysis for the s.103A dismissal claim or determine the available dismissal-compensation and uplift regime.
evidence: D20 item 20.3, p.5: Ferris asks what happens if the certificate goes to HSE without anyone saying when it was made; the solicitor says that would be misleading.
D20 item 20.3, p.5: CPS/Coldbrook expressly rely on R v Cox and Railton, Barclays Bank plc v Eustice and JSC BTA Bank v Ablyazov.
D19 procedural note, p.3: the report was served before CPR 35.4 permission, which was not granted until 16 April 2025.
D18 p.1 and items 18.1-18.6: automatic dismissal and detriment are pleaded, and the reason or principal reason is expressly the central disputed issue.

scores.name: Reasoning in the alternative
scores.justification: The answer does reason in the alternative in several genuine areas of uncertainty: certificate provenance, the three audio readings, the disputed purpose and personal detriment from surveillance, the board minute, and the phone disclosure to HSE. Its treatment of the D13 date discrepancy is particularly clear. However, it manufactures an uncertainty about the contents of D20.3 despite the full text being in the bundle, and it does not fairly work through the tenable iniquity-exception case arising from the actual final question in that note and the subsequent unqualified production.
evidence: D20 item 20.2, p.3, gives three tenable readings of the words at 02:40.
D13 Part 4 gives a 1 December installation date; D18 item 18.1 gives a 16 November internal disclosure and D01 para.20 gives a 17 November HSE call.
D09 Part 2 says the file was generated on 13 November but cannot exclude re-typing of a genuine earlier certificate.
D20 item 20.3, p.5, is complete rather than an unidentified or unseen document.

scores.name: Asserted vs said vs shown vs established
scores.justification: The answer generally uses disciplined formulations such as "Meridian says", "Mr Aksoy says", "the record shows" and "the tribunal must determine", and it correctly treats the preliminary HSE report as provisional rather than established fact. It sometimes overstates evaluative conclusions, for example treating the surveillance as likely unlawful and the whistleblowing claim as likely successful without consistently restating that purpose and dismissal reason remain disputed. The more serious lapse is its unsupported characterisation of D20.3 as having unknown possible contents.
evidence: D01 para.33: the preliminary report "should not be treated as evidence of the truth" of recorded matters.
D18 item 18.6: the purpose of monitoring, whether clause 9 was a detriment, and the reason or principal reason for dismissal are disputed.
D13 Part 4: Meridian's Article 6 basis was first advanced in its ET3 and its purpose is expressly disputed.

scores.name: Determinative silences
scores.justification: The answer identifies several potentially determinative missing matters, including the native recording and metadata, the content and knowledge of the HSE telephone call, and the manuscript board-minute materials, and proposes focused disclosure or forensic enquiries. It does not present these as a clear set of at least three determinative silences, and it incorrectly treats the contents of D20.3 as such a silence. It should also have identified the absence of direct evidence from Ashgrove-Pike, the unproduced camera footage, and the missing original Version A handover as distinct determinative gaps.
evidence: D20 item 20.2 is a solicitor-prepared transcript; the bundle does not exhibit the native audio or extraction metadata.
D18 item 18.6: Meridian's knowledge of the 17 November HSE call is disputed; D18 does not reproduce the call's content.
D18 item 18.2: the alleged manuscript original board minute has not been produced.
D08 Part 1: the paper original of Version A has not been produced; D13 Part 3: footage from cameras 3, 4 and 7 was not produced.

scores.name: Completeness
scores.justification: Every numbered sub-question is addressed, and the answer supplies forum tables throughout, with appropriate recognition that PACE section 78 is a Crown Court issue and CPR 31.20 and CPR Part 35 are primarily TCC matters. It also addresses the requested professional-conduct issue and gives practical orders. The score is reduced because the DPA 2018 issue is expressly deferred rather than answered, the s.103A burden and remedies/uplifts analysis is incomplete, and the privilege conclusion does not properly resolve the required alternative case.
evidence: D20 p.1: the CPR 31.20 application is listed for 14 November 2025.
D19 p.3: the TCC permission issue and criminal service position are separately recorded.
D18 p.1: the claims include s.103A dismissal, s.47B detriment, wages and contractual notice.

questions.overallComment: This is a well-structured and generally well-cited answer, with sound instincts on evidential reliability, forum distinctions and the need for preservation orders. Its central weakness is that it fails the bundle's contradiction exercise: it identifies far fewer than fifteen contradictions and almost never gives the required comparative probative assessment. The treatment of D20.3 is materially flawed because the answer claims not to have its contents although the full note is reproduced, and that error infects its privilege and iniquity analysis. The legal advice is also incomplete on the named iniquity authorities, the s.103A burden and remedies, and the DPA 2018 point.
